# perfproof

You find where the user's code can get faster, and you prove which
changes really are, keeping only those. The user speaks plain language
and never has to type a perfproof command. You run the `perfproof` CLI
for everything that must be exact, and you do the thinking.

Run it as `perfproof <command> --json`. If `perfproof` is not on PATH,
use `uvx --from git+https://github.com/siddiquifaras/perfproof perfproof`.
Read only the JSON fields named here; never paste the CLI's own text to
the user.

## How to talk

- Plain sentences, no jargon. One next step at the end of every stop,
  as a question with at most two options, your recommendation first,
  for example "Shall I <recommended>, or <alternative>?"
- Three kinds of statement, never mixed up:
  - **Facts**: tests passed or failed, outputs identical or different,
    a count ("236 queries became 10"). Say them plainly.
  - **Estimates**: any timing that is not a calibrated KEEP or REJECT.
    Give the number and its range and say "estimate". Never call an
    estimate faster, slower, quicker, shorter, longer, a speedup, a gain,
    a win, better, worse, positive or negative, never use it as a
    reason to keep a change, and never compare it with a claim
    ("larger than claimed", "matches the 50x claim"). Do not use
    these words even to say you are not using them or to describe an
    idea's room to improve: say "the cap is 1.04x" or "it is 3% of
    the run". Say the claim can't be checked until perfproof can
    give a verdict.
  - **Verdicts**: only from `compare`, only when
    `verdict.calibration == "calibrated"`. Only then say "kept" or
    "faster".
- Until perfproof is calibrated, every compare ends INCONCLUSIVE with
  `verdict.diagnostics.procedure_uncalibrated: true`. Say: "perfproof can't keep
  changes yet. The estimate is X (range A to B), not yet a verdict." Do
  not offer to rerun it: a rerun cannot change that.
- Before anything is decided, name a goal by its metric ("the time
  the `rolling_sum` calls take") and the bar as a line ("the low end of
  the range must be above 3%"), never as "faster" or "beats".
- A cap from a profile ("the most this function could save") is a
  bound, never a promise: say "can save at most 10x", never "10x
  faster". See [discovery.md](discovery.md).
- A question you will go on from once it is answered (which workload,
  the spec, a branch, a busy machine) gets no `Result:` line. A stop
  that ends the session (not a git repository, uncommitted changes,
  nothing to run) and every finished run end with one last line, the
  only place the word "Result" appears as a label: never use it as a
  heading or bold label in the body ("**Result:**"); head the timing
  paragraph "**The timing:**" as in messages.md. When `compare` returned a
  verdict, copy it: `Result: <verdict.outcome> (<verdict.reason>)`,
  adding `, gate <verdict.gate>` when there is one, for example
  `Result: INCONCLUSIVE (insufficient_evidence)` or
  `Result: REJECT (correctness, gate correctness)`. A REJECT from a
  gate (correctness, lock, side_effects, runtime, procedure, same_host)
  is a verdict: copy it. Use `Result: NO VERDICT (<plain
  reason>)` only when `compare` returned no verdict at all (you stopped
  before it, or it answered `ok: false`). An uncalibrated INCONCLUSIVE
  is "not yet a verdict" to the user, but `compare` did return one:
  its line is `Result: INCONCLUSIVE (<verdict.reason>)`, never NO
  VERDICT.

## What the user asked for

Look at what the user wrote when they asked for perfproof:

1. `light`, `medium` or `full` as the first word sets the depth (below).
2. Nothing else: find speedups in this project (**find**).
3. A branch, commit, PR or diff named as the whole request, a URL, or
   marked ("pr 123", "branch x", "this diff", "my changes"): **prove** it.
4. A file or function: find speedups starting there.
5. Anything else is a description ("the CSV import is slow"): find
   speedups for that. If it names an existing branch or PR, ask once
   whether to prove it instead.

Depth decides how much you explore: how many ideas and attempts. It
never changes how a change is measured or what counts as kept.

| Depth | Find | Prove |
|---|---|---|
| `light` | one workload, one profile, the top one or two ideas, one attempt | default for proving |
| `medium` (default for find) | the workload the user cares about, the top three to five ideas across the angles | the same, plus the claim check |
| `full` | every angle in discovery.md, several attempts | every candidate in the branch, one at a time |

Before a `medium` or `full` run, say in one sentence that it uses more
of their agent budget than `light`, and offer `light`. Remember their
answer in `.perfproof/preferences.json`.

## Before anything runs

Check these in order; the first one that fails speaks, and you stop
with one sentence and one next step:

1. Not a git repository with a commit: ask them to commit.
2. Finding speedups with uncommitted changes (ignore `.perfproof/`):
   ask them to commit or set them aside. Never stash, reset or commit
   for them. Proving a change does not need a clean tree.
3. The workload needs a service (database, cache, API) that is not on
   this machine: stop. Offer a local copy; never point a benchmark at
   anything remote.
4. `perfproof doctor --json` warns (`high_load`, `on_battery`,
   `low_power_mode`, `thermal_limit`, `non_performance_governor`): this
   is how real machines are, not a reason to stop. Say what it means in
   one sentence, carry on, and put the conditions in the report. The
   old and new versions run in alternating rounds, so load that hits
   both mostly cancels; it only widens the range. Offer to wait only if
   the user would rather. When finding speedups, mention it in the one
   question of step 1.
5. The project has no tests or other check of the result: say a change
   can't be kept without one, and offer to write a check (the output on
   a fixed input) with the user's agreement. If they decline, still
   measure; perfproof reports the estimate and says it can't keep.

Never set `allow_runtime_change`, `allow_cross_host` or any other
opt-in in a spec without asking; each one turns a check off.

You write only to `.perfproof/` and, once the checks pass and the user
agrees, to one branch `perfproof/<name>` for kept changes. Never commit
to, rewrite or edit a branch the user named or owns; a fix you write for
their change goes on a new `perfproof/<name>` branch. Before you
finish, remove files your own runs created in the user's tree (outputs,
caches) that were not there when you started, and leave `git status`
as you found it apart from that branch.

## Prove a change

No discovery. One candidate at a time, against its parent.

1. Work out the baseline (the commit the change started from, usually
   `git merge-base`) and the candidate (a revision, or the working
   directory for uncommitted changes). Show the diff stat. If commits
   the user did not write are in it, ask which to prove.
2. List what the change claims (commit message, PR text): faster how
   much, at what. Quote each claim word for word in quotation marks
   rather than restating it. You will check each claim or say it was
   not checked.
3. Reuse a locked benchmark if one runs the changed code: each
   directory under `.perfproof/benchmarks/` is one, and
   `perfproof bench list <name> --json` shows its versions. Otherwise
   write one: a command that runs the changed code the way it is really
   used, plus the test command and the output files to compare
   ([spec.md](spec.md)), and lock it with
   `perfproof bench define <name> --spec <file> --json`. A script you
   write for it goes in `.perfproof/harness/`, never in the user's
   tree. If you can't find any command that runs the changed code,
   stop and say so (nothing can be measured without one).
   If the change edits code AND adds or edits a benchmark, never lock a
   file the change touches: copy the benchmark into
   `.perfproof/harness/` (the baseline's version if it has one, else the
   change's new file) so both versions run the identical benchmark, and
   lock that copy. If the change touches only benchmark or test files,
   build the spec on them as usual and let `compare` judge it.
   Once `bench define` has locked a file, never edit it: if the
   benchmark needs fixing, write a corrected copy under a new name,
   define that, and compare with it.
   Never refuse a change on your own reading of the diff, even when it
   plainly edits the benchmark or its tests: run `compare`, which
   refuses such a change in seconds at its lock check and records why.
   A refusal must come from perfproof, never from you.
4. Run `perfproof compare <name> --candidate <rev or dir> --baseline
   <rev> --json`, adding `--spec-hash <hash>` when the benchmark has more
   than one version (error `ambiguous_hash`). It can take minutes;
   say so before you start. Never end your turn while it runs: wait for
   its JSON, then report.
5. Report from the JSON with [messages.md](messages.md): what was
   checked and passed (only gates in `gates[]` with their `status`),
   what failed, the estimate (`verdict.estimate`, range
   `verdict.interval.lower` to `verdict.interval.upper`; never
   `diagnostics.wall_interval`) or verdict, what was not checked, and
   where the run record is (`report_path`). Never say a check ran
   unless `gates[]` shows it. "Not checked" comes from the JSON's
   `not_verified` list: say each item in plain words and, where one
   exists, what would make the change keepable ("run the program
   directly instead of through a shell script"). Offer only a step that
   would actually change the item. When the `coverage` reason names
   lines ("... lines 12-14 never ran"), say those changed lines never
   ran under any check and offer a test that reaches them and fails on
   the original (a new spec, the user's call; messages.md R-5). When it
   says no coverage command is declared or no report was written, say "perfproof can't see which
   {language} lines ran" and don't offer a test for it. If `measured_metric` is set, say what was
   actually measured ("instructions weren't available here, so wall
   time was measured"). An unverified item is not a failure: the
   change was measured, it just can't be kept until that is checked.

## Find speedups

1. **Understand, then ask once.** Run `perfproof init --json` (once
   per repository; it writes only `.perfproof/`). It proposes
   `targets[]`, `workloads[]` and goals, each with an `id` and its
   evidence, and `questions[]` for what it could not find out. Look for
   the project's own benchmarks first (a `benchmarks/` or `bench/`
   directory, asv, pytest-benchmark, `cargo bench`, `go test -bench`,
   JMH, benchmark.js or tinybench) and prefer one that exercises what
   the user asked about; with no target named, propose the path the
   project's own benchmarks and README point at, and say why. Prefer a
   workload that runs the project's most-used public entry points
   over the first or most niche benchmark in a list: a function that
   every call goes through only shows up when the workload makes many
   different calls. Profile the same workload you will measure. Prepare
   everything before you ask: your suggested answer to each question
   that matters (what "faster" means, what must not change), the spec
   built on them ([spec.md](spec.md)) or a locked benchmark that fits
   (one directory per benchmark under `.perfproof/benchmarks/`), and
   the branch `perfproof/<name>` where attempts will go. Then ask in
   one message, your suggestion first for each: the workload and
   answers, the spec in one paragraph, permission for the branch, and
   any machine warning from the checks above. On their yes, confirm in
   this order, since each needs the one before:
   `perfproof project confirm <target id> <workload id> --json`, then
   `perfproof project goal <workload id> --metric <m> --confirm --json`
   (`<m>` is `wall`, `cpu`, `p99`, `memory`, or the name of a metric
   your benchmark reports, with `--direction` and `--unit`), then lock
   the spec. Nothing is measured on a workload the user has not
   confirmed. After that, don't stop again before the report unless
   something comes up that only the user can decide.
2. **Profile.** For Node or TypeScript code read [node.md](node.md)
   first: how to launch, warm up and profile it. `perfproof profile
   <name> --json`. Print the top 15
   entries of `result.hotspots[]` in the order the CLI gives them
   (by self share), one per line as `function file line
   self_fraction total_fraction`, not a cut of the whole output, and
   read them with the wall versus CPU time. Print the top 15 of
   `result.frames_by_total[]` the same way: frames by time spent under
   them, including ones with no self time. A project function
   (`is_library` false) high there and low or absent in `hotspots` is
   a candidate: its time is in the calls it makes, so call it less or
   make those calls cheaper. If most of the profile is interpreter
   start-up or
   imports, the workload does too little work per run: make it do
   more (a loop of calls inside the process, a larger input) and
   profile again before choosing an idea. If CPU is well below wall, the program is mostly
   waiting: look at I/O and services, not loops. For a native
   program, profile it through `perfproof profile` with the native
   recorder in [native.md](native.md) (`--profiler-command`, `--own-module
   <binary>`): it starts the program itself and samples it by process
   id, on macOS and on Linux, so nothing has to be installed. Do not
   look a process up by name (`pgrep`, `sample <name>`, `ps`): in a
   restricted environment those fail, and the result would be a profile
   perfproof did not make. If the recorder itself fails, read its error
   and fix the command before falling back to anything else; if you must
   sample by hand, use the pid of a child you started, call each
   function's share an estimate, name the sampler, and say perfproof's
   profile did not run.
   For Java and other JVM code, read [java.md](java.md) first: how to
   launch the benchmark so the runtime is identified, how to warm it
   up, how to profile it, and what usually goes wrong.
   For Rust, read [rust.md](rust.md) first: how to launch the built
   binary so the toolchain is identified, what a first run costs, how to
   profile it, and what usually goes wrong.
   For Go, read [go.md](go.md) first: how to build and launch the
   benchmark so the runtime is identified, how to profile it with
   pprof, and what usually goes wrong.
   For Ruby, read [ruby.md](ruby.md) first: how to launch it so the
   runtime is identified, how YJIT and the collector enter the noise,
   how to profile it with stackprof, and what usually goes wrong.
   For C# and other .NET code, read [csharp.md](csharp.md) first: how to
   build and launch the application, how the tiered JIT enters the
   noise, how to profile it with dotnet-trace, and what usually goes
   wrong.
   For C and C++, read [native.md](native.md) first: how to build and
   launch the benchmark so the toolchain is identified, how to profile
   it with `sample` or `perf`, how to check the change ran, and what
   usually goes wrong.
3. **Ideas.** For each hotspot, work out the most a change there could
   save (the cap in [discovery.md](discovery.md)). For a Python
   function, measure the cap rather than estimate it:
   `perfproof measure <name> --stub <module>:<function> --json` gives
   `result.stub.cap_bound`, or the reason no cap can be given in
   `result.stub.cap_withheld`; then use the profile's share instead
   and say the cap comes from the profile. For
   growth with input size, `--sizes 1,2,4,8 --size-arg=--n=<base>`; for
   one setting, `--set NAME=VALUE`. These are bounds and estimates, not
   verdicts. Drop any idea whose cap is at or below `1 + min_effect`
   from the spec. Check the angles in discovery.md for ones the profile
   hints at. Check `git log` for what was tried before.
4. **Cheap test first.** Before writing a real change, test the idea
   cheaply (the cheapest check that would prove it wrong). Drop ideas
   it refutes and say why as a mechanism you read in the code or a
   count you made ("the lookup rebuilds a dict on every call"), never
   as a timing or a word like "slower" or "no quicker". A timing you
   took yourself (`time`, a loop, a stopwatch, even "about 23 ms") only
   decides what to try next: never report it to the user. Report counts or a bound
   instead ("the stage is 18% of the run, so it can save at most
   1.2x").
5. **Try.** Create the branch the user allowed in step 1 (ask now
   only if they did not) from the commit the user was on, write the
   change there, as small as the idea needs, commit it on that branch,
   and prove it exactly as above with `--baseline <that commit>
   --candidate perfproof/<name>`. Every attempt uses that same
   baseline.
6. **Keep or undo.** First switch back to the branch the user was on,
   so their working tree is exactly as it was. A KEEP stays on
   `perfproof/<name>`. An attempt whose checks failed is undone by
   deleting its branch, which only you created; never touch anything
   else. While perfproof can't give verdicts yet, an attempt whose
   checks all passed stays on its branch for the user to judge: say the
   checks passed and the speed is not decided, and offer to delete it.
   Never argue from the estimate.
7. **Report** once at the end ([messages.md](messages.md)): each idea,
   its evidence, what happened, what was kept, what was not checked,
   and what to try next. Say "nothing left could clear the bar" only
   when no idea with a cap above the bar is left untried; otherwise
   say what this depth tried, which ideas remain with their caps, and
   offer the next depth (at `full`, say what you would try next).

Keep notes for the next session in `.perfproof/session.md`: each idea,
its cap, its cheap test and its outcome, one line each. Read it before
trying an idea: an idea refuted before on unchanged code is not retried
without saying what differs.

## Spend the user's budget well

- Fewer turns: take the next step in the same turn when nothing needs
  an answer.
- Read one function, not the whole file; never re-read a file you have.
- Never read raw logs, profiler files, `record.json` or `samples.npz`;
  the JSON fields above are enough. Give the path if the user wants
  more.
- Use a semantic code search tool if one is installed, `grep` if not.
- Write a helper script once, show it, reuse it.

1	# Rust
2	
3	Read this when the code to speed up is Rust, built with cargo. The
4	method is the same as everywhere else; what differs is how to launch
5	the benchmark so the toolchain can be identified, what first runs cost
6	(there is no JIT), how to profile compiled code, and where Rust code
7	usually loses time.
8	
9	## Launch the benchmark so the toolchain can be identified
10	
11	`compare` only keeps a change when it knows what runs each version. It
12	reads a built binary: the compiler that made it is in the file. It does
13	not follow `cargo run`, `cargo bench`, `rustc` or `rustup`: rustup
14	chooses the toolchain (a `rust-toolchain.toml` can change it), and
15	`cargo run` builds before it starts the program, which would put the
16	build inside the timed run. Those give `runtime` `not_available` and a
17	KEEP is withheld. Build in `setup`, which is not timed and not checked,
18	and run the binary itself:
19	
20	```json
21	"setup": {"commands": [["cargo", "build", "--release", "--locked"]],
22	          "timeout_seconds": 1800},
23	"command": ["target/release/<name>", "<arguments>"]
24	```
25	
26	- Always `--release`, and `--locked` so the dependencies are the ones
27	  in `Cargo.lock`. A `target/debug` binary is unoptimised code, and
28	  rarely what the user runs: say so if the user's own command is one.
29	- Give both versions the same build: the same `cargo` command, features
30	  and `RUSTFLAGS`. A change to the `[profile]` in `Cargo.toml`
31	  (`lto`, `codegen-units`, `opt-level`, `panic`) is part of the change
32	  under test, and perfproof does not compare it between the two trees;
33	  read it in the diff, and say that a change of it is a change of the
34	  build and not of the code.
35	- A library crate has no binary. Write a small harness crate under
36	  `.perfproof/harness/bench/` with the crate as a path dependency and an
37	  empty `[workspace]` table (so cargo does not take it for a member of
38	  the project's workspace), run `cargo generate-lockfile --manifest-path
39	  .perfproof/harness/bench/Cargo.toml` once before locking (a lockfile
40	  written later would change the locked directory), and build it in
41	  `setup` into a directory of its own:
42	
43	  ```
44	  ["cargo", "build", "--release", "--manifest-path",
45	   ".perfproof/harness/bench/Cargo.toml", "--target-dir",
46	   "target/perfproof-bench"]
47	  ```
48	
49	  The command is then `target/perfproof-bench/release/bench`. Pass the
50	  inputs and results through `std::hint::black_box`, or the compiler
51	  may fold a constant loop away.
52	- Native code and the project's own tests are run the usual way: the
53	  `correctness` command may be `cargo test --release --locked`.
54	
55	## Warm-up
56	
57	Compiled Rust has no JIT, so there is no in-process warm-up to wait
58	for and no stop rule to write. Two small effects remain; the numbers
59	are in "Warm-up (Rust)" of `docs/method.md`, from one busy machine:
60	
61	- The first execution of a freshly built binary was several times
62	  slower than later ones in one macOS series. Set the spec's `warmup`
63	  to at least 1, as a precaution.
64	- The first iterations inside one process were slower than most later
65	  ones in one busy-machine series, which did not separate a warm-up from
66	  noise. If the benchmark loops in process and prints one number
67	  (`reported`), discard its first few iterations (5 is a guess) and
68	  loop a fixed number of times. Never loop until the time settles: a
69	  loop that can fail to settle must not fail the execution.
70	
71	A command line tool is measured whole (`wall`); a library function is
72	looped in process.
73	
74	## Profile
75	
76	`perfproof profile` runs any command that writes folded stacks. The
77	system profilers write their own formats, and Rust symbols arrive
78	mangled, so `perfproof.profilers.rust` runs the binary under `sample`
79	(built into macOS) or `perf` (Linux) and writes folded stacks with
80	demangled symbols:
81	
82	```
83	perfproof profile <name> --json --own-module <binary name>
84	  --profiler-command '["<python>", "-m", "perfproof.profilers.rust",
85	  "record", "--output", "{output}", "--project-root", "<repo root>",
86	  "--", "{command}"]'
87	```
88	
89	`<python>` is the Python that perfproof itself runs in: the `python`
90	beside the `perfproof` executable. `--own-module` is the binary's file
91	name: the profile then marks the crates that the repository defines
92	(the `Cargo.toml` files under the root name them) as project code, and
93	the standard library, the dependencies and C code linked in as library
94	code.
95	
96	What to know when reading the result:
97	
98	- A frame is ``<binary>`<crate>::<module>::<function>``. There is no
99	  file or line: a Rust path says where to look (`my_crate::parse::tokens`
100	  is in the crate `my_crate`, module `parse`, so `src/parse.rs`, or
101	  `src/parse/mod.rs`, or an inline `mod parse`). `grep` for the
102	  function.
103	- The command must be the built binary. A command that starts the
104	  binary through `cargo run` or a shell is profiled as cargo or the
105	  shell.
106	- On macOS `sample` records every thread, running or parked, from a few
107	  tens of milliseconds after the start; the wrapper drops threads parked
108	  in a blocking call and says how many samples that was on stderr. The
109	  share is of the samples kept. A run of well under a second gives few
110	  samples: run the workload longer. On Linux the CPU-clock event counts
111	  only running threads, and a stack needs frame pointers: build the
112	  profiled binary with `RUSTFLAGS="-C force-frame-pointers=yes"` into
113	  its own `--target-dir` (the timed binary stays as it was), or add
114	  `"--call-graph", "dwarf"` to the command (not run here; it needs debug
115	  information in the binary). In a container, libc frames
116	  can show as `[unknown]`, and frames in the kernel as `[kernel]`.
117	- The compiler inlines. A small function called in a loop has no frame
118	  of its own: its time is in the caller, and a hot caller whose body is
119	  one loop is the answer. The same holds for the standard library
120	  (`Vec::push`, `contains`), where the growth or the comparison shows
121	  only if it was not inlined.
122	- Neither profile shows time a thread spends waiting (macOS: the
123	  wrapper drops parked threads; Linux: the event counts running time
124	  only): if CPU time is well below wall time, look at locks and I/O,
125	  not at the loops.
126	
127	## What usually goes wrong, and the cheap test for each
128	
129	Run the test on the profile's top frames before writing a change. Each
130	is a count or a share, never a timing to report.
131	
132	| Suspect | What the profile shows | Cheap test |
133	|---|---|---|
134	| Growing a `Vec` or `String` that has a known length | allocator frames (`realloc`, `_szone_realloc`) high; `RawVec` growth frames (`finish_grow`, `do_reserve_and_handle`) where not inlined | count allocations per call with the allocator below; `with_capacity(n)` or `reserve(n)` leaves one |
135	| Cloning, `to_vec`, `to_owned`, `collect` into a temporary | allocator frames (`malloc`, `free`, `__rdl_alloc`) at the top, and `<String as Clone>::clone`; the cloning function's own share small | the allocation count per call against the number of items: one per item means a copy per item; borrow (`&[T]`, `&str`, `Cow`) instead |
136	| Formatting in a loop (`format!`, `to_string`, `println!` to build text) | `core::fmt::` frames plus allocator frames | allocations per call; `write!` into one reused `String` allocates nothing per item |
137	| Iterator chains | nothing named: adapters inline into the caller. 175	## Coverage
176	
177	`-C instrument-coverage` and the toolchain's `llvm-profdata` and
178	`llvm-cov` give an lcov report. Build a second, instrumented binary in
179	`setup`:

181	```
182	["env", "RUSTFLAGS=-C instrument-coverage", "cargo", "build", "--release",
183	 "--locked", "--target-dir", "target/perfproof-cov"]
184	```
185	
186	(the build itself was run by hand with that `RUSTFLAGS`, not through
187	perfproof's `setup`),
188	
189	then `python -m perfproof.bench.rust_coverage --output <file>.lcov
190	--project-root <repo root> -- target/perfproof-cov/release/<name>

198	## When to stop
199	
200	As in [discovery.md](discovery.md): when the top frames are the
201	standard library's or an allocator's own and the project's share is
202	small, the cap says what is left. A benchmark whose rounds disagree
203	widely is noisy, not slow; say so and report the range.

1	# Writing the benchmark spec
2	
3	perfproof measures one command, the benchmark, and checks one test
4	command. You write both into a JSON spec and lock it with
5	`perfproof bench define <name> --spec <file> --json`. Locking records the
6	hashes of the files listed in `harness`, `oracle`, `inputs` and
7	`config`, so a later change that edits them is refused.
8	
9	Keep the spec file in `.perfproof/specs/<name>.json`. Show the user the
10	command, the test command and what is compared, in one short paragraph,
11	before you lock it.
12	
13	## Choosing the benchmark
14	
15	- It runs the code the user cares about, the way it is really used, on
16	  realistic input. Not a microbenchmark of one line.
17	- One run is long enough to be far above the timer's step, and short
18	  enough that dozens of runs fit in the time the user will wait. Tell
19	  the user the expected total before you start.
20	- It is deterministic: fixed seeds, fixed input files, no network.
21	- If the code under test has its own timing, have the benchmark print
22	  one line `PERFPROOF {"value": <seconds>}` on stdout and use the
23	  `reported` metric. That times only the work, not interpreter start-up.
24	  Otherwise use `wall`.
25	
26	## Where the benchmark lives
27	
28	The baseline is a fresh checkout of the commit, so a file you wrote and
29	did not commit is not in it. Put a benchmark you wrote under
30	`.perfproof/harness/` (for example `.perfproof/harness/bench_x.py`) and
31	list it in `harness`. perfproof copies that directory, byte for byte,
32	into both versions before anything runs, and a change cannot touch it.
33	Once one file there is listed, every file in the directory is locked,
34	so put helper modules beside the benchmark and expect an edit to any of
35	them after locking to be refused. Only `.git` and `__pycache__` are
36	ignored: any other file that appears or changes there after the freeze
37	(a cache the benchmark writes beside itself, a `.DS_Store`) fails the
38	lock gate, so tell the benchmark to write caches outside that directory.
39	That includes a candidate directory the user hands you: its own
40	`.perfproof/harness/` is replaced, so keep nothing of theirs there.
41	Run it from the repository root with `cwd` `"."`.
42	
43	Do not point the command at `.venv/bin/python` or another ignored path
44	without `setup`: the baseline checkout has no such directory. Add
45	`"setup": {"commands": [["uv", "sync", "--frozen"]], "timeout_seconds":
46	600}`, which builds each version's own environment, and run the
47	benchmark with `uv run --frozen python ...` (plain `uv run` may
48	re-resolve) or `.venv/bin/python ...`, which then
49	exists in both. Never use the main checkout's environment: an editable
50	install there would import its source in both versions.
51	
52	## Choosing the checks
53	
54	- `correctness.command`: the project's tests for that code, or the whole
55	  suite if it is fast. A failing test on the new code rejects the change.
56	- `correctness.outputs`: files the benchmark writes that must be the
57	  same in both versions. Use `numbers` for numeric output (with a
58	  tolerance only if the user says results may differ slightly), `text`
59	  or `bytes` otherwise. Make the benchmark write its result to a file
60	  if it doesn't.
61	- `correctness.coverage_command` (optional, with
62	  `correctness.coverage_timeout_seconds`): only for a change in a
63	  language other than Python, and only when the project has a coverage
64	  tool. A command that runs the tests under it and writes lcov or
65	  Cobertura to the path in `$PERFPROOF_COVERAGE_REPORT`. Python needs
66	  none. Leave it out when unsure: changes in other languages are then
67	  measured but not kept, with "no coverage command declared".
68	
69	## Template
70	
71	```json
72	{
73	  "schema_version": 4,
74	  "name": "<name>",
75	  "command": ["python", "bench.py", "--output", "out/result.npy"],
76	  "cwd": ".",
77	  "env": {},
78	  "metric": {"kind": "reported", "direction": "lower_is_better", "unit": "s"},
79	  "objective": "wall_time",
80	  "guardrails": [
81	    {"metric": "peak_memory", "direction": "lower_is_better", "unit": "bytes",
82	     "allowance": 0.1, "allowance_source": "default"},
83	    {"metric": "peak_gpu_memory", "direction": "lower_is_better", "unit": "bytes",
84	     "applicable": false, "reason": "no GPU is used"},
85	    {"metric": "p99_latency", "direction": "lower_is_better", "unit": "s",
86	     "applicable": false, "reason": "serves no requests"}
87	  ],
88	  "correctness": {
89	    "command": ["python", "-m", "pytest", "-q", "tests/test_thing.py"],
90	    "cwd": ".",
91	    "timeout_seconds": 300,
92	    "outputs": [{"path": "out/result.npy", "compare": "numbers"}]
93	  },
94	  "warmup": 1,
95	  "budget": {"max_rounds": 60, "max_seconds": 1800},
96	  "looks": {"n0": 10, "k": 10, "max_looks": 6},
97	  "min_effect": 0.03,
98	  "alpha": 0.05,
99	  "timeout_seconds": 120,
100	  "harness": ["bench.py"],
101	  "oracle": ["tests/test_thing.py"],
102	  "inputs": [],
103	  "config": [],
104	  "allow_runtime_change": false,
105	  "allow_cross_host": false
106	}
107	```
108	
109	## Fields worth knowing
110	
111	- `command`: run a Python script, or a program built in the
112	  repository. A shell in between (`sh -c`, a `.sh` script) or an
113	  installed program outside the repository can't be identified, and
114	  the runtime check refuses it.
115	- `metric.kind`: `wall` (whole command), `cpu`, `reported` (the
116	  `PERFPROOF` line), `counter` (Linux only). `wall` and `cpu` are in
117	  seconds and lower is better.
118	- `guardrails`: list all three as above. Mark one `applicable: false`
119	  with a short true reason when it does not apply.
120	- `setup`: `{"commands": [[...], ...], "cwd": ".", "timeout_seconds": N}`.
121	  Argv commands run once in each version before the first run, outside
122	  the timing, with the same environment as the benchmark. It must not
123	  need credentials or a remote service.
124	- `reset`: if the benchmark changes something outside its own process
125	  (a local database, a cache directory), add
126	  `"reset": {"command": [...], "timeout_seconds": 60}` to put it back
127	  before every run.
128	- `budget` and `looks`: use the template's values (60 rounds, `n0` 10,
129	  `k` 10, `max_looks` 6), the provisional defaults the decision rule is
130	  calibrated under. Depth changes how many ideas you try, not these.
131	  `n0` and `k` must be even.
132	- `min_effect`: the bar. A change is kept only if even the low end of
133	  its range beats `1 + min_effect` (3% by default). Change it only if
134	  the user states a different bar.
135	- `harness`, `oracle`, `inputs`, `config`: the benchmark files, test
136	  files, input data and config files to lock. Paths relative to the
137	  repository. Those under `.perfproof/harness/` are installed in both
138	  versions by perfproof. Never lock the code you are trying to speed
139	  up, or any file the change you are proving touches: a change to a
140	  locked file is refused, so the change could never be measured. A
141	  benchmark the change adds or edits goes into `.perfproof/harness/` as
142	  a copy instead (see SKILL.md, prove step 3).
143	
144	If `bench define` refuses the spec, its JSON `error.message` says why.
145	Fix that field; don't loosen a check to get past it.
146

1	# What to tell the user
2	
3	Build every message from the `compare --json` fields, never from the
4	CLI's own text. Short sentences. End with one next step and the
5	`Result:` line.
6	
7	## The report after a compare
8	
9	Use this shape, leaving out empty parts:
10	
11	> **What I checked:** <facts: "your 42 tests passed on both versions",
12	> "the output file is identical", "236 queries became 10">.
13	>
14	> **The timing:** <estimate or verdict, see below>.
15	>
16	> **Not checked:** <every entry of `not_verified`, plus any gate
17	> whose status is `waived`, in plain words: "whether every changed line
18	> ran under a test", "memory use", "whether both versions ran the same
19	> Node">, with what would make it checkable where there is one.
20	>
21	> **Conditions:** <only if `doctor` warned or `warnings` names load:
22	> "measured on a busy machine (load 7)"; omit otherwise>.
23	>
24	> **Run record:** `<report_path>`.
25	>
26	> <one next step>
27	>
28	> `Result: <outcome> (<reason>[, gate <gate>])`
29	
30	## The timing line, by result
31	
32	Read `verdict.outcome`, `verdict.reason`, `verdict.rule`,
33	`verdict.gate`, `verdict.calibration` and `verdict.diagnostics`. Say
34	"the bar" as the number from the spec, `1 + min_effect` (3% by
35	default). Ratios are old time divided by new time; say so once.
36	
37	`compare --json` carries `not_verified`, `warnings` and
38	`measured_metric`, but not yet which tests failed, which output
39	differs, or guardrail values. For those, read only the "Correctness"
40	section of `report.md`.
41	
42	| Result | Say |
43	|---|---|
44	| INCONCLUSIVE with `verdict.diagnostics.procedure_uncalibrated` (every run today) | "perfproof can't keep changes yet. The estimate is <estimate>x (range <lower> to <upper>), which is not a verdict. The change is <where it is>." Never set the estimate against the change's own claim. |
45	| INCONCLUSIVE with `verdict.diagnostics.coarse_resolution` | "The benchmark is too short for the timer to tell the versions apart. A longer input would fix that." |
46	| INCONCLUSIVE, calibrated, rule 5 | "Undecided: the range <lower> to <upper> still includes the bar (<bar>)." |
47	| INCONCLUSIVE, rule 2, `not_verified` has `coverage` naming lines that never ran | "The changed lines <file>:<a>-<b> never ran under any check, so perfproof can't tell whether they broke anything. Add a test that reaches them (it must fail on the original), or leave this change for you to judge?" Say "never ran" from the reason; a new test is a new spec and a new baseline, the user's call. |
48	| INCONCLUSIVE, rule 2 (a check could not run, or a guardrail could not be established) | "Measured, but not kept: <each `not_verified` item> couldn't be checked here. <What would make it checkable.>" Don't mention the range or the bar. |
49	| KEEP, calibrated | "Kept: <estimate>x faster (range <lower> to <upper>), clear of the bar (<bar>). It's on `perfproof/<name>`." |
50	| REJECT `performance` | "Not kept: even the high end of the range, <upper>x, doesn't clear the bar (<bar>)." Say "slower" only if `verdict.regression` is true. |
51	| REJECT `guardrail` | "Not kept: it uses more <memory or latency> than allowed (<value> against <limit>)." |
52	
53	## Refusals (a check failed, so speed doesn't matter)
54	
55	| `verdict.gate` | Say |
56	|---|---|
57	| `correctness` | "Refused: the new version changes the result. <failing tests, capped at five, or which output differs>." |
58	| `lock` | "Refused: the change edits the benchmark or its tests, so the measurement would no longer mean the same thing." Describe what the edit does as work, not speed: "it makes the benchmark do a quarter of the work and leaves `held_orders` unchanged", never "it runs shorter", "it speeds up the benchmark" or "rather than a speedup": nothing was timed. |
59	| `side_effects` | "Refused: the benchmark would talk to something that isn't on this machine, <address>. I can set up a local copy." |
60	| `runtime` | "Refused: the two versions wouldn't run the same program (<why>), so timing them says nothing." |
61	| `procedure`, `same_host` | "Refused: the setup differed between the two runs. I'll fix it and run again." |
62	
63	## Errors from the CLI
64	
65	When `ok` is false, say what happened in one sentence from
66	`error.message`, never the raw code, then the next step:
67	
68	- `broken_baseline`: "The original code doesn't run as set up, so I
69	  can't compare against it." Show the command and the last few lines
70	  of its output.
71	- `not_built`: "That part of perfproof isn't built yet." Do the step by
72	  hand if you can, and say so.
73	- Anything else: fix the cause if it is in what you wrote (the spec,
74	  the command); otherwise stop and tell the user.
75	
76	`Result: NO VERDICT (<plain reason>)` whenever no verdict exists.
